question:
(a) What is an intrinsic semiconductor? Explain the formation of electron-hole pairs in it.
(b) Why is the number of electrons equal to the number of holes in an intrinsic semiconductor?

options.A:
(a) An intrinsic semiconductor is a heavily doped semiconductor in which only holes conduct.
(b) The number of electrons is greater than holes because covalent bonds create electrons alone.
options.B:
(a) An intrinsic semiconductor has no covalent bonds and has free electrons at all temperatures.
(b) Electrons and holes have unrelated concentrations.
options.C:
(a) An intrinsic semiconductor is a pure semiconductor such as Si or Ge, with no intentional impurity. Thermal energy breaks some covalent bonds, promoting an electron to the conduction band and leaving a hole behind.
(b) Each broken bond creates exactly one electron and one hole, so $n_e=n_h=n_i$; both carriers contribute to conduction.
options.D:
(a) An intrinsic semiconductor is an insulator with an infinite energy gap.
(b) Holes are absent because electrons never leave covalent bonds.
